notes:
Coverage is uneven. I ran out of searches and fetches before I could get verse-level comments on vv. 24, 28–30, 32–33, 35–36, 40, 42 and 44–46, so those verses rely mostly on Enduring Word's section notes. The main Precept Austin page only loaded its introduction, so I only have the bits that turned up in search snippets. I found no material from the Catholic, Orthodox, Pentecostal or Lutheran sites, from the modern scholarship sites (bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org), or on prosperity or word-of-faith teaching for this passage. So those sections are left out, as you asked.

---

**Background for vv. 24–46**
- Moses skips Israel's earlier complaints (Numbers 11–12) and goes straight to the rebellion at Kadesh. It was this which led to the nation being doomed to wander in the wilderness until the generation that came out of Egypt had died. https://biblehub.com/deuteronomy/1-19.htm
- Ellicott says Moses mentions the eleven-day journey (v. 2) to show how rebellion turned a short trip into many wearisome years. https://biblehub.com/deuteronomy/1-2.htm
- J. Vernon McGee says Moses retells what the fathers went through so the new generation might profit from them rather than repeat the failures. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-1-commentary

**vv. 24–25**
- Guzik: the spies brought back proof of how good the land was, not just a report, including some of the remarkable fruit in Canaan. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-1/
- Guzik also argues the spying showed doubt. God had already said the land was good, so unless they did not believe Him, there was no reason to confirm it on their own. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/archives/guzik_david/StudyGuide_Deu/Deu_1.cfm
- McGee: God had said it was a good land. The real problem was unbelief. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-1-commentary

**v. 26**
- Precept Austin: the command to go in and possess the land had already been given in vv. 8 and 21. God gave no exceptions for big walls or big people. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-1-commentary
- Guzik: "Nevertheless" (NKJV) is a haunting word. It was the exact word in the mouth of the ten fearful spies (Numbers 13:28). https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/archives/guzik_david/StudyGuide_Deu/Deu_1.cfm

**v. 27**
- Bob Utley: here the people are impugning the motives and nature of God, and they had forgotten what He had done for them on the journey from Sinai. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-1-commentary
- Guzik: they could not name one time God had let them down, yet they answered God's faithfulness with rebellion, murmuring, and unbelief. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/archives/guzik_david/StudyGuide_Deu/Deu_1.cfm

**v. 28**
- A Precept Austin note (on vv. 19–28) says the scouts claimed the Canaanites, including the Nephilim, were too strong to fight, and that the ten scouts convinced the people the land could not be taken (Numbers 13:32–33). https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-1-commentary

**vv. 29–31**
- Keil & Delitzsch: Moses' own appeal is left out of Numbers 13 because it failed. "Goeth before you" in v. 30 is picked up again in v. 33. "Bore thee" means God supported, tended, and provided for thee in the most fatherly way. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/1-31.htm
- Gill (Baptist): God carried them in his arms, in his bosom, with great care and tenderness. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/msg/deuteronomy/1-31.html
- Calvin: the picture is of bearing because the way would have been by no means passable unless God had borne them, as it were, on His shoulders. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/1-31.html
- Matthew Henry: Moses once complained that he had to carry the people like a nursing father (Numbers 11:12). Here he admits it was God who carried them. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/1-31.html
- Ellicott ties v. 31 to Acts 13:18, where God is said to have borne Israel like a nursing father in the wilderness. https://biblehub.com/deuteronomy/1-31.htm

**vv. 32–33**
- Benson on vv. 31–34: So they could not enter in, because of unbelief. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/1-31.htm
- G. Campbell Morgan (quoted by Guzik): Israel was not left to find its own way. God went ahead and chose every campsite. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-1/
- Pulpit Commentary homiletics: God's guidance comes from day to day - just sufficient to show us present duty. https://biblehub.com/sermons/deuteronomy/1-31.htm

**vv. 34–36**
- Guzik: because Israel did not trust God's love, God swore an oath (Psalm 95:11) that the adults who left Egypt would die in the wilderness. The only exceptions were Caleb and Joshua, the two faithful spies. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-1/
- Matthew Henry (quoted on StudyLight): what kept them out was not the golden calf or any broken law but their disbelief of that promise which was typical of gospel grace. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/1-34.html

**v. 37: Why was Moses excluded? (the main interpretive question)**
- **The usual view (out of time order):** Moses was barred at Meribah about 37 years later (Numbers 20), not at the first Kadesh rebellion. Pulpit Commentary calls the verse parenthetical. It also says the Hebrew for "on your account" means an occasion or reason. https://biblehub.com/deuteronomy/1-37.htm
- Barnes (Presbyterian) agrees. He says Moses mentions it here to prick the people's conscience. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/1-37.html
- Constable: Moses wanted to emphasize spiritual lessons. He was exhorting the Israelites to action more than teaching them history. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/1-37.html
- Ellicott: the reason was the same for Moses and the people, unbelief (Numbers 20:12 and v. 32). https://biblehub.com/deuteronomy/1-37.htm
- **Is Moses shifting blame?** Calvin (Reformed) says no. Moses had fallen because he was overwhelmed by their obstinate wickedness, so it was fair to tell the people God's anger came through their sin. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/1-37.html
- Keil & Delitzsch also say he was not excusing himself. Deuteronomy 32:51 names his sin. Here Moses focuses on the people's guilt to wake up their consciences. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/1-37.htm
- Gill (Baptist): it happened at the same place but nearly 38 years later, when the people provoked him to speak rashly. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/1-37.htm
- Adam Clarke (Wesleyan) only points readers to his notes on Numbers 20:12. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/1-37.html
- So among the Reformed, Baptist and Wesleyan writers I found, there is no real disagreement on this verse.
- **Modern critical view:** The Cambridge Bible (George Smith, whom Precept Austin calls a "radical liberal") says many scholars treat vv. 37–38 as added by an editor. It reads Deuteronomy as teaching that Moses shared the people's guilt at the first Kadesh rebellion. It sees the Meribah explanation as a later "priestly" view that each person dies for their own sin. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/1-37.htm and https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-1-resources
- **A Catholic translation:** the Douay-Rheims version of v. 37 adds a phrase saying God's anger at the people was no wonder, since He was angry with Moses too. https://biblehub.com/deuteronomy/1-37.htm

**v. 38**
- Guzik: God told Moses to encourage the man who would replace him. Moses' work of bringing Israel to Canaan would be finished through Joshua. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-1/
- Calvin: "stands before you" means Joshua was Moses' servant. That made the punishment plainer, since by an entire inversion, a successor is given to Moses, who had been his servant. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/calvin/comment3/comm_vol06/htm/ii.xxii.htm
- Keil & Delitzsch: even in anger God kept His covenant by giving the people a new leader. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/1-37.htm

**v. 39**
- Guzik: the people's excuse was that their children would die (Numbers 14:3). God's answer was "You will be killed, and your children will possess the land." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-1/
- Calvin: limiting this grace to small children shows that everyone old enough to reason shared in the crime. He links the phrase to Jonah 4:11, where God spares little ones who cannot yet judge. https://studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/1-39.html
- Gill: "in that day" is stressed because those children were now the adults Moses was speaking to, 38 years later. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/1-39.htm
- Constable connects the phrase to Adam and Eve: the new generation, like the first parents, had to depend on God as a gracious father. https://studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/1-39.html
- **Popular "age of accountability" use:** GotQuestions uses this verse to say God holds people responsible only when they can tell right from wrong. https://www.gotquestions.org/age-of-adulthood.html
- A Bible Hub article is more careful: the verse does not establish a definite age of accountability, but it shows God's compassion toward children. https://biblehub.com/q/bible's_view_on_age_of_accountability.htm
- The Cambridge Bible notes that Numbers 14:29 sets the line at age 20. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/1-39.htm

**v. 40**
- Coffman: this sentenced the adults to the forty years. Very little is recorded about those years because when people have rebelled against God, all of their activities lose the quality of significance. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/1-37.html

**vv. 41–43**
- Guzik: Israel changed its mind but went out in its own strength, not in faith. It rebelled again while supposedly repenting. Their sorrow was about the consequences, not about grieving God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-1/
- Guzik quotes Merrill: once Canaan was forbidden, the people decided that was exactly what they would do. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-1/
- William Kelly: there may be a thorough spirit of disobedience at the very time that people talk of doing whatever God is pleased to command. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/1-37.html

**v. 44**
- Guzik: an attack made in their own wisdom and strength ended in disaster. He reads "like a swarm of bees" as meaning great numbers. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-1/

**v. 45**
- Matthew Henry: the Lord would not listen to them because they would not listen to Him. Like Esau, they found no place of repentance, though they sought it carefully with tears. He contrasts worldly sorrow with godly sorrow. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/1-37.html
- Guzik: they wept only after the defeat, and again over the consequences rather than over distrusting God's love. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-1/

**v. 46**
- Guzik: Deuteronomy says nothing more about these years. Numbers records only Korah's rebellion, more complaining, Miriam's death and Meribah. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-1/
- A Precept Austin note says Kadesh became the main campsite for the next 38 years (Deuteronomy 2:14). https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-1-commentary

**Two small things for the writers**
- Guzik's two editions differ on vv. 41–43. Enduring Word says "thirty-eight more years" in the wilderness, while the older Blue Letter Bible study guide says "forty."
- Precept Austin lists further sources I couldn't read, including Spurgeon on v. 25 and v. 38, Calvin, Utley and Constable. They're worth checking for the gaps: https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-1-resources
